title: Differentiate masked focal loss under class imbalance
task: Implement multiclass focal loss: mean of -alpha[y]*(1-p[y])**gamma*log(p[y]) over valid rows, normalized by the number of valid targets, not the sum of class weights. Use log-softmax, preserve autograd and return graph-connected zero when every target is ignored. Reject nonfinite logits, invalid shapes/dtypes/labels, negative or nonfinite gamma, and nonpositive/nonfinite class weights. Do not detach the focal factor.
concept: Focal weighting changes which examples dominate the gradient. The factor depends on the current model probability and must participate in autograd; multiplying cross entropy by a detached difficulty score defines a different update. A declared reduction also matters when class weights and ignored examples interact. This Lab uses multiclass logits, one integer target per row and a fixed valid-row denominator. It exercises extreme scores and an entirely ignored batch without introducing undefined gradients.
review: Compare gamma zero with cross entropy, then inspect derivatives at a difficult example. Explain why class weighting, focal weighting and resampling are different interventions. Measure rare-group errors on held-out data before choosing them.

checks.name: gamma zero matches the declared weighted reduction
checks.code:
from torch.nn import functional as F
x = torch.tensor([[2.0, 0.0], [1.0, 3.0]], dtype=torch.float64)
y = torch.tensor([0, 1])
a = torch.tensor([2.0, 4.0], dtype=x.dtype)
assert torch.allclose(focal_loss(x, y, 0, a), F.cross_entropy(x, y, weight=a, reduction='sum') / 2), 'Contract failed: gamma zero matches the declared weighted reduction.'

checks.name: focal factor participates in the gradient
checks.code:
x = torch.tensor([[0.3, -0.4]], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
y = torch.tensor([1])
focal_loss(x, y).backward()
actual = x.grad[0, 0].item()
h = 1e-05
p = x.detach().clone()
m = p.clone()
p[0, 0] += h
m[0, 0] -= h
assert abs(actual - (focal_loss(p, y) - focal_loss(m, y)).item() / (2 * h)) < 1e-07, 'Contract failed: focal factor participates in the gradient.'

checks.name: ignored rows and empty valid batch retain finite gradients
checks.code:
x = torch.randn(3, 2, requires_grad=True)
y = torch.tensor([-100, 1, -100])
assert torch.allclose(focal_loss(x, y), focal_loss(x[1:2], y[1:2])), 'Contract failed: ignored rows and empty valid batch retain finite gradients.'
z = focal_loss(x, torch.full((3,), -100))
z.backward()
assert z.item() == 0 and torch.equal(x.grad, torch.zeros_like(x)), 'Contract failed: ignored rows and empty valid batch retain finite gradients.'

checks.name: large logits and row shifts preserve the result
checks.code:
x = torch.tensor([[1000.0, -1000.0], [0.0, 2.0]], requires_grad=True)
y = torch.tensor([1, 0])
r = focal_loss(x, y)
r.backward()
assert torch.isfinite(r) and torch.isfinite(x.grad).all(), 'Contract failed: large logits and row shifts preserve the result.'
assert torch.allclose(r, focal_loss(x.detach() + 100, y)), 'Contract failed: large logits and row shifts preserve the result.'

title: Own both passes of a sharpness-aware optimizer step
task: Execute one SAM update with the supplied optimizer. closure returns a differentiable scalar loss and does not call backward. Compute the global first-pass norm, perturb trainable parameters in that direction by rho, recompute gradients, restore exact original parameter values and apply exactly one optimizer step using second-pass gradients. Always restore parameters and clear gradients if the second pass fails. Reject invalid rho, nonfinite losses/gradients, duplicate or incomplete optimizer ownership. This fixture uses deterministic layers without BatchNorm or dropout; stateful stochastic layers need a separate replay/buffer policy.
concept: Sharpness-aware training evaluates a nearby parameter vector before making the real update. Two forward passes are not two optimizer steps. The second gradient belongs to the perturbed model, while momentum and weight decay must update the original model exactly once. Reversing a floating-point perturbation by subtraction can leave rounding residue, so this exercise owns exact snapshots. Exception handling is part of the algorithm: a failed closure must never leave the live model perturbed.
example:
import torch
w = torch.tensor([3., 4.])
print(w / w.norm())
review: Explain which gradient is used and when optimizer state advances. A stochastic or stateful model additionally needs an explicit policy for randomness and running buffers; passing this deterministic fixture does not resolve that policy.

checks.name: analytic quadratic uses the perturbed gradient once
checks.code:
m = torch.nn.Linear(1, 1, bias=False)
with torch.no_grad():
    m.weight.fill_(2)
o = torch.optim.SGD(m.parameters(), lr=0.1)
r = sam_step(m, o, lambda: m.weight.square().sum(), 0.5)
assert abs(m.weight.item() - 1.5) < 1e-06 and abs(r['norm'] - 4) < 1e-06, 'Contract failed: analytic quadratic uses the perturbed gradient once.'

checks.name: closure runs twice but momentum advances once

m = torch.nn.Linear(1, 1, bias=False)
o = torch.optim.SGD(m.parameters(), lr=0.1, momentum=0.9)
calls = []

def closure():
    calls.append(1)
    return m.weight.square().sum()
sam_step(m, o, closure, 0.1)
assert len(calls) == 2 and len(o.state) == 1 and ('momentum_buffer' in o.state[m.weight]), 'Contract failed: closure runs twice but momentum advances once.'

o = torch.optim.SGD(m.parameters(), lr=0.1)
r = sam_step(m, o, lambda: m.weight.square().sum(), 0.1)
assert r['norm'] == 0 and m.weight.item() == 0, 'Contract failed: zero first gradient remains finite.'

title: Project conflicting task gradients without mutating their owners
task: Return a detached [tasks, parameters] matrix of PCGrad gradients. For each task, visit the other ORIGINAL task gradients in a seed-local shuffled order. If the current projected gradient has a negative dot product with an original peer, remove that component. Skip zero-norm peers. Do not mutate the input or global RNG. The caller chooses how to combine the projected rows; this Lab does not assert that a mean improves every task.
concept: Multi-task objectives can produce gradients that oppose one another even when the shared model is differentiable. PCGrad edits a task gradient by removing conflicting components relative to original peer gradients. Projection order matters with three or more tasks, so order and randomness are part of the reproducibility contract. Returning separate rows preserves the distinction between surgery and the later task-weighting decision. This is a local vector algorithm; it does not claim a Pareto optimum or execute distributed reduction.
example:
import torch
a = torch.tensor([1., -1.])
b = torch.tensor([0., 1.])
print(torch.dot(a, b))
review: Compare original and projected directions on several task geometries. Audit parameter alignment, missing gradients and aggregation weights before applying surgery to real shared and task-specific model parameters.

title: Update a detached Group DRO adversary from group means
task: Return (robust_loss, next_log_weights). All G declared groups must occur in this batch. Average losses within each group, update adversary log weights by eta times DETACHED group means, normalize in log space, then weight differentiable group means by detached updated probabilities. Do not backpropagate into old adversary state. Reject empty/missing/out-of-range groups, nonfinite losses/state and nonpositive eta. This deliberately balanced-batch contract avoids silently inventing loss for unobserved groups.
concept: Average risk can hide a poorly served subgroup when that group is rare. Group DRO maintains an adversary over declared groups, increasing mass on groups with larger observed mean loss. The adversary state is an optimization state, not a differentiable shortcut through every previous batch. Normalizing by each group count prevents duplicated rows from becoming an unintended group weight. Observing only a subset of groups requires an explicit estimator; this exercise instead declares complete group coverage per batch.
review: Separate group definition, adversary optimization and final evaluation. Compare average and worst-group held-out results with an ERM baseline; training group weights alone are not evidence of robustness under unseen shifts.

checks.name: adversary uses group means and normalized log state
checks.code:
x = torch.tensor([1.0, 1.0, 3.0], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
r, q = group_dro(x, torch.tensor([0, 0, 1]), torch.zeros(2, dtype=x.dtype), 0.5)
w = torch.tensor([0.5, 1.5], dtype=x.dtype).softmax(0)
assert torch.allclose(q.exp(), w) and torch.allclose(r, w @ torch.tensor([1.0, 3.0], dtype=x.dtype)), 'Contract failed: adversary uses group means and normalized log state.'

r.backward()
assert torch.allclose(x.grad, torch.stack([q.exp()[0] / 2, q.exp()[0] / 2, q.exp()[1]])) and old.grad is None and (not q.requires_grad), 'Contract failed: only sample losses receive gradients.'

title: Fit a positive heteroscedastic Gaussian likelihood
task: Use variance=softplus(raw_variance)+floor and return mean(0.5*(log(2*pi)+log(variance)+(target-mean)**2/variance)). Preserve gradients through both mean and raw variance. Require aligned nonempty finite floating tensors and finite floor>0. The floor is part of the declared model; do not clamp a negative variance after taking its logarithm.
concept: A regression model can learn both a conditional mean and input-dependent noise. Gaussian likelihood rewards a good mean but also penalizes excessive variance, unlike simply enlarging every interval. An unconstrained raw output is transformed into a positive variance before any logarithm or division. Very negative raw values test the numerical behavior at the floor. The learned quantity is aleatoric uncertainty under this likelihood assumption; it does not include model uncertainty or automatically provide calibrated prediction intervals.
example:
import torch
from torch.nn import functional as F
raw = torch.tensor([-50., 0., 3.])
print(F.softplus(raw) + 1e-4)
review: Keep variance distinct from standard deviation. Evaluate log loss and interval coverage on held-out data, and inspect results by region; a good average likelihood can coexist with subgroup miscalibration.

y = torch.tensor([2.0, 0.0], dtype=m.dtype)
expected = (0.5 * (math.log(2 * math.pi) + v.log() + (y - m).square() / v)).mean()
assert torch.allclose(gaussian_nll(m, raw, y), expected, atol=1e-12), 'Contract failed: matches the independent Gaussian density.'

title: Train through per-channel fake quantization and saturation
task: Implement symmetric signed per-output-channel fake quantization of floating [out,in] weights with qmax=2**(bits-1)-1 and qmin=-qmax, bits in 2..8. Infer detached scales=max(abs(channel))/qmax with floor 1e-8, or accept explicit finite positive detached [out] scales. Round ties to even, simulate quantize/dequantize in floating point and use straight-through rounding with zero gradient outside the clipping interval. Return a floating tensor; this is QAT simulation, not a packed int8 kernel or a speed benchmark.
concept: Quantization-aware training simulates rounding during training so the model can adapt to a finite grid. Rounding has almost-everywhere zero derivative; a declared straight-through rule supplies the training surrogate. Saturation still needs a policy: this exercise passes gradients inside the representable interval and stops them outside it. Per-channel scales prevent one large output row from determining every row’s resolution. The result remains floating point and is not evidence of compressed storage, integer execution or faster inference.
review: Inspect clipping rates, the scale calibration set and post-conversion error separately. Compare a floating baseline with a real deployed quantized runtime before claiming memory or latency savings.

assert torch.allclose(fake_quant_weight(w, 4), expected), 'Contract failed: per-channel grids match an independent quantizer.'

assert torch.equal(w.grad, torch.tensor([[0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.0]])) and s.grad is None, 'Contract failed: surrogate gradients stop outside explicit clipping limits.'

title: Differentiate response-masked Direct Preference Optimization
task: Inputs are finite floating [batch,2,time,vocab] logits and int64 [batch,2,time] aligned response targets; pair index 0 is chosen, 1 rejected, and -100 masks non-response positions. Sum valid token log probabilities for each response, not their length average. Return mean(softplus(-beta*((policy_chosen-policy_rejected)-(reference_chosen-reference_rejected)))). Detach all reference logits. Every response needs a valid target. Reject bad labels, shape, empty batches and nonpositive/nonfinite beta. This is the DPO objective, not a claim of aligned behavior from passing a small fixture.
concept: DPO compares the policy’s chosen-versus-rejected log-probability margin with a frozen reference margin. Summing only response targets keeps prompt and padding positions out of that comparison. Length normalization would change the objective, rather than merely improve numerical stability. Softplus evaluates the binary preference likelihood without explicitly taking a logarithm of a near-zero sigmoid. Reference ownership is observable in autograd: an accidental gradient into the reference changes the optimization problem even when the scalar loss initially looks correct.
example:
import torch
from torch.nn import functional as F
margin = torch.tensor([-1000., 0., 1000.])
print(F.softplus(-margin))
review: Audit pair identity, response masks, length bias and preference provenance. A decreasing preference loss does not by itself establish helpfulness, safety or generalization to new prompt groups.

checks.name: equal policy and reference yield log two

import math
p = torch.randn(2, 2, 3, 4, dtype=torch.float64)
y = torch.tensor([[[1, 2, -100], [0, 1, 2]], [[0, 1, 2], [2, -100, -100]]])
assert abs(dpo_loss(p, p.clone(), y, 0.7).item() - math.log(2)) < 1e-12, 'Contract failed: equal policy and reference yield log two.'

checks.name: independent summed-token margin matches the objective

from torch.nn import functional as F
p = torch.tensor([[[[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 2.0]], [[0.0, 1.0], [2.0, 0.0]]]], dtype=torch.float64)
r = torch.zeros_like(p)
y = torch.tensor([[[0, 1], [0, -100]]])
ps = p.log_softmax(-1)
rs = r.log_softmax(-1)
m = ps[0, 0, 0, 0] + ps[0, 0, 1, 1] - ps[0, 1, 0, 0] - (rs[0, 0, 0, 0] + rs[0, 0, 1, 1] - rs[0, 1, 0, 0])
assert torch.allclose(dpo_loss(p, r, y, 0.3), F.softplus(-0.3 * m)), 'Contract failed: independent summed-token margin matches the objective.'

title: Own grouped advantages and the clipped policy surrogate
task: Implement the GRPO-style clipped surrogate core for [prompts,completions,tokens] sampled log probabilities. Use detached within-prompt reward advantages normalized by population standard deviation plus 1e-8. Compute exp(logp-old_logp.detach()), take the minimum of unclipped and [1-clip,1+clip] clipped ratio times advantage, average over valid tokens within each response, then equally over prompts/completions. Detach rewards. Require each response to contain a token, at least two completions, 0<clip<1 and absolute log-ratio<=20. This exercise isolates the surrogate; rollout collection, a reference-KL penalty and reward design are separate components.
concept: Grouped policy optimization compares completions of the same prompt rather than fitting a value baseline. Reward normalization must use that prompt’s group, and old policy scores are immutable evidence from rollout collection. Clipping limits the surrogate incentive after a ratio crosses a boundary, with different signs for good and bad advantages. Per-response token reduction prevents long completions from acquiring accidental extra weight. The Lab deliberately separates this mechanism from an end-to-end RL training system.
example:
import torch
rewards = torch.tensor([[1., 3., 2.]])
a = rewards - rewards.mean(-1, keepdim=True)
print(a / (rewards.std(-1, correction=0, keepdim=True)+1e-8))
review: Inspect constant-reward groups, stale rollout policies and response masks. Normalizing rewards is not a substitute for an informative reward function, a reference policy or an evaluation protocol.

title: Handle multiple positives and singleton anchors in SupCon
task: Normalize finite nonzero [N,D] embeddings, exclude self pairs from every softmax denominator, and average log probability over all same-label non-self positives for each anchor. Average only anchors that have a positive; singleton embeddings still appear as negatives for other anchors. Require N>=2, aligned int64 labels, temperature>0, and at least one positive pair. Preserve gradients to every participating embedding. Avoid zero times negative infinity on masked diagonals.
concept: Pairwise contrastive learning assigns one positive per observation; supervised contrastive learning can assign several. Averaging individual positive log probabilities differs from taking the logarithm of their summed probability. A singleton label has no positive anchor loss but can still be a useful negative for another class. Removing its entire row and column would change the objective. Masked numerical operations also matter: multiplying an invalid diagonal by zero can still propagate NaNs.
example:
import torch
labels = torch.tensor([0, 0, 1])
same = labels[:, None] == labels[None, :]
print(same & ~torch.eye(3,dtype=torch.bool))
review: Review positive identity and augmentation policy separately from class labels. Test invariance to joint permutation and positive scaling, then assess representation quality on a genuinely held-out downstream task.

checks.name: independent categorical sum over all positives
checks.code:
import math
x = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.0], [0.9, 0.1], [0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]], dtype=torch.float64)
y = torch.tensor([0, 0, 1, 0])
z = x / x.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True)
scores = z @ z.T / 0.4
values = []
for i in range(4):
    positive = [j for j in range(4) if j != i and y[j] == y[i]]
    if positive:
        den = sum((math.exp(scores[i, j].item()) for j in range(4) if j != i))
        values.append(sum((math.log(den) - scores[i, j].item() for j in positive)) / len(positive))
assert abs(supervised_contrastive(x, y, 0.4).item() - sum(values) / len(values)) < 1e-10, 'Contract failed: independent categorical sum over all positives.'

checks.name: singleton remains a negative and receives gradients
checks.code:
x = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.2], [0.8, 0.3], [0.1, 1.0]], requires_grad=True)
r = supervised_contrastive(x, torch.tensor([0, 0, 1]), 0.5)
r.backward()
assert torch.isfinite(x.grad).all() and x.grad[2].abs().sum() > 0, 'Contract failed: singleton remains a negative and receives gradients.'

checks.name: joint permutations and positive scaling preserve loss
checks.code:
x = torch.tensor([[1.0, 0.2], [0.8, 0.3], [0.1, 1.0], [0.2, 0.9]])
y = torch.tensor([0, 0, 1, 1])
p = torch.tensor([2, 0, 3, 1])
assert torch.allclose(supervised_contrastive(x, y, 0.4), supervised_contrastive(x[p] * 3, y[p], 0.4), atol=1e-06), 'Contract failed: joint permutations and positive scaling preserve loss.'

title: Route sparse top-two experts with an explicit capacity policy
task: For finite floating [tokens,dim] x, a Linear router with E>=2 outputs and E Linear experts of one common output width, choose the two largest router softmax probabilities per token (ties by expert index). Process tokens in input order; accept an assignment while that expert has capacity. Renormalize the retained gates per token. A token whose two assignments overflow returns graph-connected zeros. Return (output, auxiliary, accepted_loads, dropped_assignments). Auxiliary is E*sum(mean_full_router_probability*detached_pre_capacity_top2_fraction), fractions normalized by 2*tokens. Execute only accepted expert rows; do not evaluate every expert densely. Reject invalid shapes, nonfinite inputs/parameters and nonpositive integer capacity.
concept: A sparse router introduces a discrete ownership decision between differentiable computations. The selected gate probabilities remain trainable, but selection indices and capacity decisions do not. Overflow policy changes which examples reach which expert; this exercise makes input-order admission and renormalization explicit. Load balancing uses pre-capacity assignments so dropping work cannot masquerade as balanced demand. CPU execution demonstrates correctness and gradients, not expert-parallel communication, a distributed all-to-all operation or an inference speedup.
example:
import torch
p = torch.tensor([[.2, .6, .2]])
print(p.argsort(descending=True, stable=True))
review: Inspect requested versus accepted loads, dropped work and gate gradients. Define a production overflow policy and measure expert utilization before choosing a capacity factor or claiming sparse efficiency.

router=torch.nn.Linear(2,3)
experts=torch.nn.ModuleList([torch.nn.Linear(2,2) for _ in range(3)])
x=torch.tensor([[1.,0.],[0.,1.],[1.,1.]],requires_grad=True)
output,aux,loads,dropped=sparse_mixture(x,router,experts,2)
result=output.square().mean()+.1*aux
result.backward()

title: Preserve target mass with speculative accept and residual resampling
task: Implement one exact categorical speculative step for normalized finite nonnegative [vocab] probabilities. The proposed token must have positive draft mass. Accept it when accept_uniform < min(1,target[proposal]/draft[proposal]). On rejection, inverse-CDF sample from normalized clamp(target-draft,min=0), using residual_uniform and right-open CDF bins. Return (token, accepted). Uniforms are explicit finite values in [0,1), so the function owns no RNG. Reject invalid probabilities, token indices and uniforms. This single-position probability mechanism makes no wall-clock speed claim.
concept: A draft model proposes cheaply, but naive verification would change the target distribution. Speculative sampling accepts some draft mass and compensates on rejection using the positive residual between target and draft probabilities. That residual is not simply the target distribution again. Making both uniform draws explicit separates the probability transform from RNG ownership and permits deterministic boundary tests. The Lab studies one categorical verification step, not a multi-token cached transformer execution pipeline.

title: Search a finite-state grammar with explicit EOS and sequence scores
signature: constrained_beam(logits, transitions, start, accepting, eos, width=4)
task: Search finite floating [time,vocab] position-conditioned logits under transitions[state][token]=next_state. EOS is permitted only in accepting states and terminates the hypothesis without a transition. Use original full-vocabulary log-softmax scores before grammar filtering: do not renormalize each allowed subset. Keep finished hypotheses without scoring further tokens, sort by descending accumulated score then lexicographic token sequence, and retain width hypotheses after each step. Return {tokens,score} for the best finished hypothesis; reject if none finishes. Wide beams can match exhaustive search; a finite narrow beam is not guaranteed optimal.
concept: A grammar constrains valid sequences, while a language model supplies their scores. Filtering illegal transitions after normalizing the original vocabulary preserves the declared model likelihood; renormalizing only legal tokens instead creates a different conditional distribution. Finished EOS paths need their own lifetime, otherwise they can be accidentally extended or charged extra probability. This finite-position exercise makes search and grammar correctness inspectable without a remote model. A narrow beam can still prune the best complete sequence.
review: Compare a wide beam with a brute-force oracle on short sequences. Define termination, tie breaking and length scoring before adding history-dependent model calls or claiming that beam search finds the global optimum.

checks.name: wide beam matches exhaustive allowed complete sequences
checks.code:
import itertools
x = torch.tensor([[2.0, 1.0, -2.0], [1.0, 2.0, -1.0], [0.0, 0.0, 3.0]], dtype=torch.float64)
tr = {0: {0: 1, 1: 1}, 1: {0: 1, 1: 1}}
scores = x.log_softmax(-1)
candidates = []
for length in (2, 3):
    for prefix in itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=length - 1):
        tokens = prefix + (2,)
        score = sum((scores[i, t].item() for i, t in enumerate(tokens)))
        candidates.append((tokens, score))
best = sorted(candidates, key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]))[0]
r = constrained_beam(x, tr, 0, {1}, 2, 20)
assert tuple(r['tokens']) == best[0] and abs(r['score'] - best[1]) < 1e-12, 'Contract failed: wide beam matches exhaustive allowed complete sequences.'

title: Project: train uncertainty and calibrate independent prediction intervals
task: Build the complete local synthetic heteroscedastic regression experiment with four disjoint partitions: training, validation selection, conformal calibration and final test. Train both mean and positive variance using Gaussian NLL, choose the checkpoint by validation NLL, then compute normalized absolute calibration residuals and the finite-sample ceil((n+1)*(1-alpha)) order statistic without interpolation. Calibration and test labels must never fit or select model weights. Keep the full reference report schema. Marginal conformal coverage requires exchangeability and does not imply subgroup coverage.
concept: An uncertainty model and an interval calibration procedure answer different questions. This project trains a heteroscedastic likelihood, selects its checkpoint on validation data, and only then uses a separate calibration partition to choose interval width. The corrected order statistic is an integer rank, not an interpolated percentile. Final test rows measure observed coverage without feeding back into model or quantile selection. Synthetic regions make subgroup differences visible while keeping every row reproducible offline.
